<explanation>
Based on the provided file structure and README, this project is a boilerplate for a RESTful API built using Node.js, Express, and Mongoose. It is designed to serve as a starting point for building production-ready backend servers that include features such as JWT-based authentication, request validation, centralized error handling, API documentation via Swagger, logging (Winston/Morgan), and more. Below is a detailed guide on how to draw an accurate and detailed system design diagram tailored to this project's architecture.

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Client/Consumer: Although not part of the repository, external clients (e.g., browser-based apps, mobile apps, or other services) will call the RESTful endpoints.
   • API Gateway (Express Server): The heart of the system where the Express application is set up (see src/app.js and src/index.js). This handles incoming HTTP requests.
   • Routes Layer: Located in src/routes (with versioned routes under v1) that maps HTTP endpoints to controller functions.
   • Controllers: In src/controllers, these components process incoming requests, call the relevant business logic, and send responses. For example, auth.controller.js and user.controller.js.
   • Services Layer: Found in src/services, which contains the core business logic (e.g., authentication, email handling, token management, and user services). These abstract complex operations away from the controllers.
   • Models and Data Layer: Inside src/models, Mongoose models (e.g., user.model.js and token.model.js) define the data schema for MongoDB. This includes custom plugins (in src/models/plugins) like paginate and toJSON.
   • Middleware: In src/middlewares, which covers authentication, error handling, rate-limiting, input validation, etc. These components intercept requests and responses to augment functionality.
   • Configuration and Utilities: Found in src/config and src/utils. You have configuration settings such as logging, passport, tokens, and environment variables. Utilities (ApiError, catchAsync, pick) simplify common code patterns.
   • Documentation: The API documentation resources in src/docs that, when the server is running, provide a Swagger-based UI for inspecting endpoints.
   • Testing: Tests are organized under tests/ (both integration and unit tests) ensuring system quality and behavior.

2. Outline the Interactions and Relationships:
   • Externally, a client makes HTTP requests to the Express server.
   • The Express server’s routing layer directs the request to the appropriate controller based on the URL path (e.g., /v1/auth/login or /v1/users).
   • Controllers process the input and delegate work to service components. In the process, they make use of validation middleware (e.g., using Joi schemas) and check for authentication/authorization via auth middleware.
   • Business logic implemented in the services may interact with the database via Mongoose models. Here, custom plugins (like toJSON and paginate) enhance the data layer.
   • Logging middleware (using morgan and winston) and error handling middleware capture runtime information and errors.
   • For operations that need asynchronous support (for example, sending emails or token generation), the services interact with external systems or internal utilities.
   • Finally, a response is sent back to the client, optionally including API documentation endpoints for exploration.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Layered Architecture: Clear separation of concerns is maintained through controllers (presentation layer), services (business logic layer), and models (data persistence layer).
   • Middleware-driven Request Processing: Express middlewares handle authentication, error-handling, rate limiting, and data validation.
   • Modular and Pluggable: The use of plugins for Mongoose models and separate modules for validation, logging, and configuration encapsulate functionality.
   • Container & Process Management: Dockerfiles and Docker Compose files show readiness for containerized deployment, while PM2 (ecosystem.config.json) handles process management in production.
   • Comprehensive Testing: The separation of unit and integration tests reinforces a test-driven approach.
   
4. Include Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Technologies: Node.js, Express, MongoDB, Mongoose.
   • Authentication: JWT and Passport.
   • Validation: Joi.
   • Logging: Winston and Morgan.
   • Process Management: PM2.
   • API Documentation: Swagger (swagger-jsdoc and swagger-ui-express).
   • Testing: Jest.
   • Containerization: Docker and Docker Compose.
   • Code Quality: ESLint, Prettier, and Git hooks via Husky.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram (Full-stack API diagram specifics):
   • Since this is a backend RESTful API starter kit, the frontend (client) might be shown as an external consumer.
   • Emphasize the clear separation between Express (API Gateway) and individual components (routes, controllers, services, models).
   • Clearly indicate external integrations (e.g., MongoDB, email server via SMTP, external CI services like Travis CI, and Docker/CICD for deployment).

6. Instructions for the Diagram Layout:
   • Use shapes (e.g., rectangles or rounded boxes) to represent each component:
       – Label components clearly (e.g., “Express App”, “Auth Controller”, “User Service”, “Mongoose Models”, “Validation Middlewares”).
   • Draw directional arrows to illustrate the request flow:
       – From “Client” to “API Gateway (Express)” to “Routes” to “Controllers” and then to “Services” and “Models”.
       – Additionally, show middleware arrows intercepting requests either before or after controllers.
   • Use color coding or different shapes to distinguish:
       – Presentation layer (client and API endpoints)
       – Business logic (services)
       – Data layer (Mongoose models and plugins)
       – Utilities and configurations (config, logging, error handling)
   • Optionally add a legend that explains the colors and line types used (especially if you incorporate grouping for external services such as SMTP or container management tools like Docker).
   • Include configuration details (pointing out the Docker environment files, PM2 config, and environment variables) to underline deployment aspects.

7. Final Touches and Level of Detail:
   • Be very detailed by ensuring that every major directory (like controllers, services, models, and middlewares) appears as a distinct component.
   • Represent external/internal dependencies (e.g., database connection between Mongoose and MongoDB, and external authentication components like JWT and Passport).
   • Include annotations or callouts for key actions (e.g., “Validation via Joi”, “Error handling with centralized middleware”, “Logging with Winston and Morgan”).
   • The diagram should be as exhaustive as possible, breaking down the project into many small components – don’t hesitate to depict even finer details (such as separate routes under version “v1” or the role of API documentation).

By following this guide, the principal software engineer should be able to create a comprehensive system design diagram that thoroughly represents the architecture of this RESTful API boilerplate, its flow of data, and the interaction among its various layers and components.
</explanation>
